books.section: Topic 3.13 Continuity and Change in Period 3
Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals

primary_sources: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776
Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” 1790

stimulus.text:
Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776:

“I long to hear that you have declared an independency. I desire you would remember the ladies and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the husbands. Remember, all men would be tyrants if they could. If particular care and attention is not paid to the ladies, we are determined to foment a rebellion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any laws in which we have no voice or representation.”

Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, 1790 (written in 1779):

“Is it upon mature consideration we adopt the idea, that nature is thus partial in her distributions? Is it indeed a fact, that she hath yielded to one half of the human species so unquestionable a mental superiority? ... Are we deficient in reason? We can only reason from what we know, and if an opportunity of acquiring knowledge hath been denied us, the inferiority of our sex cannot fairly be deduced from thence.”
stimulus.source_note: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Founders Online, National Archives. Public domain. Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, 1790. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted from Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776, and Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” 1790, public domain.
stem: By 1800, which of the hopes in these two passages had most clearly taken shape?

options.text: Women gained a recognized civic role raising virtuous citizens.
Women won the right to vote in most of the states.
options.misconception: Women still could not vote in most states in 1800.

options.text: Husbands lost all of their legal power over their wives.
options.misconception: Husbands kept their legal power over wives after 1800.

options.text: Women took seats in Congress and in the state legislatures.
options.misconception: No woman sat in Congress or a state legislature in 1800.

rationales.A: The ideal of republican motherhood gave women a recognized civic role: raising virtuous citizens for the republic.
rationales.B: Women still could not vote in most states in 1800.
rationales.C: Husbands kept their legal power over wives after 1800.
rationales.D: No woman sat in Congress or a state legislature in 1800.
rationales.general:
1. Adams asked for laws more generous to women; Murray asked for equal schooling.
2. Neither won the vote or office for women by 1800.
3. Background from the books: what did take shape was the ideal of republican motherhood, which gave women a recognized civic role in raising virtuous citizens.
4. So of the hopes in the passages, the civic role of the mother is the one that had arrived.
Remember: match each hope against what actually followed, one by one.
